A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same preordering research, despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original optimization results, runtime measurements, LP-gap analyses, and interpretations of computed social-network preorders.

after.justification: Section 5 retains original social-network experiments and expands heuristic comparisons. Appendix A.3 also reports computed outcomes for a generated counterexample.

M1.justification: V2 introduces greedy moving in Section 4.4, adding node and equivalence-class moves and arc removals alongside insertion. V1's local search only inserted arcs. This substantially expands the search procedure; the max-dicut approximation and LP formulations remain.

E1.justification: The Twitter and Google+ ego networks and the 117th Congress network remain unchanged in coverage. V2 adds targeted synthetic GAF stress cases, including the perturbed, weighted six-node instance without ties in Appendix A.3. These provide limited additional test conditions.

E2.justification: V1 compares GDC, GAI, and GDC+GAI in its heuristic-gap experiment. V2 Figures 7–8 compare GDC, GDC+GAI, GDC+GM, GAF, GAF+GAI, and GAF+GM, introducing Böcker et al.'s GAF and refinement combinations while omitting standalone GAI. Clustering and partial-order comparators remain; LP+OCW is renamed OCW.

E3.justification: V1 evaluates CPU and GPU implementations of GAI; v2 specifies sequential, sparsity-exploiting GAI without GPU parallelization and removes the GPU comparison. V2 additionally evaluates bounds separately on 474 Twitter instances unsolved by ILP. The 500-second ILP and 100-second heuristic limits, network-weight construction, and listed hardware remain.

E4.justification: V2 adds GAF failure analyses with unfavorable tie-breaking and without ties, comparisons of GAI versus GM refinements under two initializers, and a focused analysis of heuristic-plus-OCW bounds on ILP-unsolved instances. V1's CPU/GPU acceleration analysis is removed. The illustrative network comparisons and Congress case study are retained.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 6 reports mean heuristic gaps; v2 Figure 7 labels its summaries as medians, and Section 5.1.2 adds median gaps for the unsolved subset. However, that section still calls 0.0318 a mean, leaving its precise estimator ambiguous. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 reports 499 rather than 494 solved Twitter instances and average transitivity 0.580 rather than 0.577. OCW gap closure changes from 30.1% on 308 instances to 30.4% on 313, so these are different-subset summaries. New results include GAF+GM's reported gap of 0.0318 and unsolved-subset median gaps of 0.146 for ILP versus 0.068 for best-heuristic-plus-OCW bounds. Table 1 and Congress results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: V1's original hardness theorem for values in {-1, 0, 1} and its Appendix A.2 reduction are replaced by an attributed theorem for {-1, 1} from Weller et al. V2 adds a characterization of preorders through unions of dicuts, its proof, and GAF counterexamples. The approximation and facet results remain; derandomization moves from Appendix A.3 to A.2.

C1.justification: V2 withdraws NP-hardness as an original contribution and expands the algorithmic contribution to include greedy moving. Its abstract, introduction, and conclusion position the proposed heuristics alongside existing GAF. The central approximation, polyhedral, and social-network application claims remain.

C2.justification: V1 favors GDC+GAI among its evaluated heuristics. V2 develops a quality/runtime tradeoff: GAF+GM has the best reported aggregate gap, while GDC+GAI is faster and wins on 121 Twitter instances. It also discusses GAF's lack of an approximation guarantee and the advantage of heuristic-plus-OCW bounds over time-limited ILP. The Congress interpretation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds sparse sequential GAI implementation information, GAF priority-queue details and omitted auxiliary bounds, and the exact synthetic matrix, generation recipe, and fixation trace. V1's standalone GAI pseudocode is removed. Hardware and code-access information remain, but inconsistencies in the newly printed update rules limit reproducibility.

R1.justification: V2 substantially revises positioning through the transitivity-editing literature, recognizing Weller et al.'s stronger hardness result and Böcker et al.'s existing heuristic. It adds related work on editing, order polytopes, and restricted-value hardness, and removes Yannakakis with the original reduction. This changes the account of prior contributions, beyond bibliography expansion.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introductory contribution narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. V2 adds a table of contents, expands the algorithm chapter from three to five subsections, and reorganizes the appendices. Much technical exposition remains, including the reflexivity discussion under a corrected heading.

P2.justification: V2 adds the counterexample diagram in Figure 4, replaces the heuristic-gap histogram with six-method boxplots, and redraws the runtime comparison with revised series and legends. It removes the Algorithm 2 display and relocates several figures. Most network diagrams and Table 1 retain their presentation and content.

improvement.justification: V2 improves attribution and adds an important prior-work comparator, a new search method, and broader analyses. However, Section 4.2's printed formulas and labeling rule do not reproduce Appendix A.3's fixation trace, Section 4.4 contains an incomplete class-move update, and gap summaries conflict about means versus medians. The PDFs do not establish whether these are documentation errors or affect the added results, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
